passed.title: Use ne_missing when nulls must compare as values; ne, lt and le return null for null inputs
passed.trap: `Series.ne` and `Series.lt` propagate nulls: a comparison that involves a null gives null, not `True` or `False`. When that mask is passed to `Series.filter`, the null rows are dropped without any warning, so a null-vs-value mismatch is silently missed. Use `Series.ne_missing` when two nulls should count as equal and a null against a value should count as different, or handle nulls explicitly with `Series.fill_null`.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

s1 = pl.Series("a", [333, 200, None, 5])
s2 = pl.Series("a", [100, 200, None, None])

print(s1.ne(s2).to_list())          # [True, False, None, None]
print(s1.ne_missing(s2).to_list())  # [True, False, False, True]

# Row 3 (5 vs null) silently disappears with ne
print(s1.filter(s1.ne(s2)).to_list())
print(s1.filter(s1.ne_missing(s2)).to_list())

print(s1.lt(250).to_list())  # null stays null
passed.output:
[True, False, None, None]
[True, False, False, True]
[333]
[333, 5]
[False, True, None, True]

passed.title: Series.len counts nulls; do not divide by it to get a mean
passed.trap: `Series.len` returns the total number of elements, and null values count towards that total. Aggregations such as `Series.mean` skip nulls. So a hand-rolled `s.sum() / s.len()` gives a different, wrong answer whenever nulls are present. For the number of non-null values use `Series.count` or `s.len() - s.null_count()`, or simply call `Series.mean`.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

s = pl.Series("a", [1, 2, None])

print(s.len())         # 3 (null counted)
print(s.count())       # 2 (non-null)
print(s.null_count())  # 1

print(s.sum() / s.len())    # 1.0  -- wrong
print(s.mean())             # 1.5  -- nulls ignored
print(s.sum() / s.count())  # 1.5

passed.title: Series.max and Series.min ignore NaN; use nan_max or nan_min to propagate it
passed.trap: By default, Polars ignores NaN values when computing `Series.max` and `Series.min`. A float column containing NaN can therefore report a clean-looking extreme value. NumPy users expect the opposite, because `np.max` propagates NaN. If NaN should poison the result, use `Series.nan_max` or `Series.nan_min`. Otherwise, check `Series.is_nan` explicitly before trusting the extreme.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

s = pl.Series("a", [1.0, float("nan"), 4.0])

print(s.max())      # 4.0 -- NaN ignored
print(s.min())      # 1.0
print(s.nan_max())  # nan -- NaN propagates
print(s.nan_min())  # nan
print(s.is_nan().any())  # True

passed.title: Series.log is the natural log; log(0) gives -inf and negatives give NaN, not null
passed.trap: The default base of `Series.log` is e, not 10, so code expecting a base-10 result gets silently wrong numbers. Use `Series.log10`, or pass the base explicitly as in `s.log(10)`. Invalid inputs also do not become null. In this example, zero gives `-inf` and a negative value gives NaN, so `Series.is_null` misses them; check with `Series.is_nan` and `Series.is_infinite` instead.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

s = pl.Series([100.0, 1.0, 0.0, -1.0])

print(s.log().to_list())    # natural log, not base 10
print(s.log10().to_list())  # [2.0, 0.0, -inf, nan]
print(s.log(10).to_list())

r = s.log10()
print(r.is_null().sum())      # 0 -- nothing flagged as null
print(r.is_nan().sum())       # 1
print(r.is_infinite().sum())  # 1

passed.title: Series.is_sorted expects nulls first by default
passed.trap: `Series.is_sorted` defaults to `nulls_last=False`, which means it expects nulls at the start of the Series. An otherwise ascending Series with a trailing null, which is the pandas habit of putting NaN last, reports `False`. Pass `nulls_last=True` when nulls are at the end. Pass `descending=True` to check for descending order, because the default only checks ascending.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

s = pl.Series([1, 2, None])
print(s.is_sorted())                # False -- null expected first
print(s.is_sorted(nulls_last=True)) # True

print(s.sort().to_list())  # [None, 1, 2] -- default puts nulls first
print(s.sort().is_sorted())         # True

t = pl.Series([3, 2, 1])
print(t.is_sorted())                # False
print(t.is_sorted(descending=True)) # True

passed.title: Series.is_unique is a method returning a Boolean mask, not the pandas bool property
passed.trap: In pandas, `s.is_unique` is a property that returns a single bool. In Polars, `Series.is_unique` is a method that returns a Boolean Series with one value per element. Writing `if s.is_unique:` tests a bound method, which is always truthy, so the check silently passes. Writing `if s.is_unique():` raises instead, because a Series has no single truth value. To get one bool, use `s.is_unique().all()` or `s.n_unique() == s.len()`.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

s = pl.Series("a", [1, 2, 2, 3])

print(bool(s.is_unique))  # True -- a bound method, not a check!

try:
    if s.is_unique():
        pass
except TypeError:
    print("TypeError")

print(s.is_unique().to_list())  # [True, False, False, True]
print(s.is_unique().all())      # False
print(s.n_unique() == s.len())  # False
passed.output:
True
TypeError
[True, False, False, True]
False
False

passed.title: Series.item() without an index raises unless the Series has exactly one element
passed.trap: `Series.item` called without an argument is not "give me the first value". It checks that the Series has length 1 and raises otherwise. Code like `s.filter(mask).item()` therefore breaks as soon as the filter matches zero rows or several rows. Pass an index, as in `s.item(0)` or `s.item(-1)`, when you want a specific position. Keep the no-argument form for cases where exactly one value is guaranteed.

passed.title: Series.mode can return several values in unspecified order
passed.trap: `Series.mode` returns a Series, not a scalar, and it contains every value that ties for most frequent. The default is `maintain_order=False`, so the order of those values is not guaranteed. Taking `s.mode()[0]` or `s.mode().item()` as "the" mode is therefore either non-deterministic or an error. Pass `maintain_order=True`, or sort the result, before picking an element, and handle the multi-value case explicitly.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

s = pl.Series("a", [3, 1, 3, 1, 2])

m = s.mode()
print(m.len())               # 2 -- a tie, not one value
print(m.sort().to_list())    # [1, 3] -- deterministic
print(s.mode(maintain_order=True).to_list())

try:
    m.item()
except ValueError:
    print("ValueError")
